questions.prompt: Compare quicksort, mergesort and heapsort. Explain how each works, their best, average and worst-case complexity, memory use and stability, why comparison sorting has an O(n log n) lower bound, and why real libraries use hybrids like introsort and Timsort.

expectedConcepts.label: Quicksort: partition around pivot; O(n^2) worst case
Mergesort: split, sort halves, merge; stable, O(n) extra
Heapsort: build heap, extract max; in place, not stable
Time complexity
Space complexity
Stability and cache behaviour
Introsort (std::sort) and Timsort (Python, Java objects)

questions.modelAnswer: Quicksort picks a pivot, partitions elements into smaller and larger, and recurses on both sides. Average O(n log n) with excellent cache behaviour and O(log n) stack, but a consistently bad pivot (sorted input with first-element pivot) gives O(n^2); random or median-of-three pivots make that unlikely. It is not stable. Mergesort splits in half, sorts each recursively and merges in linear time: always O(n log n), stable, but needs O(n) extra memory for arrays; it is ideal for linked lists and external sorting. Heapsort builds a max-heap in O(n) then repeatedly swaps the max to the end and sifts down: O(n log n) worst case, in place, but not stable and cache-unfriendly, so slower in practice. Any comparison sort needs Omega(n log n) comparisons in the worst case because a decision tree distinguishing all n! orderings has height at least log2(n!) ~ n log n. Libraries use hybrids: introsort (std::sort) runs quicksort, switches to heapsort if recursion gets too deep, and uses insertion sort for small ranges; Timsort (Python, Java for objects) finds already-sorted runs and merges them, giving O(n) on nearly sorted data while staying stable.

questions.title: Counting sort, radix sort and bucket sort
questions.prompt: Explain non-comparison sorts: counting sort, radix sort and bucket sort. How do they beat the O(n log n) comparison lower bound, what are their complexities and assumptions, why does radix sort need a stable inner sort, and when would you use them in practice?

expectedConcepts.label: Counting sort tallies keys in a small range
Radix sort processes digits LSD with a stable sort
Bucket sort for uniformly distributed values
Time complexity
Space complexity
Assumptions: bounded integer keys, negatives, skewed buckets
Not comparison-based, so the lower bound does not apply; use cases

questions.modelAnswer: The n log n lower bound applies only to algorithms that learn about order by comparing elements. If keys are integers in a known range, you can index by them instead. Counting sort counts occurrences of each key in an array of size k, turns counts into prefix sums giving each key's final position, then places elements (iterating from the end to keep it stable): O(n + k) time and O(n + k) space - great when k is small, wasteful when k is huge. Radix sort sorts by one digit at a time, least significant first, using a stable counting sort per digit; stability ensures ordering from earlier digits is preserved among equal current digits. For d digits in base b, time is O(d(n + b)); 32-bit integers with base 256 take four passes. Bucket sort scatters values into buckets by range and sorts each bucket; it is O(n) on average only if the input is roughly uniform, and degrades if everything lands in one bucket. Handle negatives by offsetting or sorting sign separately. Uses: sorting large arrays of integers or fixed-length keys, building suffix arrays, and GPU sorting.

questions.title: Bloom filters
questions.prompt: Explain how a Bloom filter works and why it can return false positives but never false negatives. Describe how to choose the bit array size and number of hash functions for a target false-positive rate, the operations it cannot support, and real systems that use Bloom filters.

expectedConcepts.label: Bit array; k hashes set bits on insert, check all bits on query
False positives possible, false negatives impossible
Sizing: m/n bits per element, optimal k = (m/n) ln 2; ~10 bits for 1%
Time complexity
Space complexity
Cannot delete or list elements; overfilling raises FP rate
Uses: LSM-tree SSTables, caches, crawlers; cuckoo filters

questions.modelAnswer: A Bloom filter is a bit array of m bits plus k independent hash functions. Insert: hash the item k times and set those k bits. Query: hash and check the k bits; if any is 0 the item was definitely never inserted, if all are 1 it is probably present, because other items may have set those bits. So there are false positives but never false negatives. Both operations are O(k) regardless of the number of items, and the structure stores no items at all. With n items, the false-positive rate is about (1 - e^(-kn/m))^k; the optimal number of hashes is k = (m/n) ln 2, and about 9.6 bits per element gives a 1% rate (each extra ~4.8 bits divides it by ten). Two hash functions combined as h1 + i*h2 are enough in practice. Limitations: you cannot delete (clearing a bit could remove other items - counting Bloom filters use small counters instead), cannot list members, and the false-positive rate climbs if you insert more than planned. Uses: LSM-tree databases (Cassandra, RocksDB) keep one per SSTable to skip disk reads for absent keys, web crawlers track seen URLs, and CDNs avoid caching one-hit wonders. Cuckoo filters support deletion with similar space.

questions.title: Skip lists
questions.prompt: Explain the skip list data structure. How do multiple levels of linked lists give expected O(log n) search, insert and delete, why is randomisation used instead of rotations, and why do systems such as Redis sorted sets and LevelDB memtables use skip lists instead of balanced trees?

expectedConcepts.label: Sorted linked list with express lanes at higher levels
Random level per node (coin flips, p = 1/2 or 1/4)
Search moves right then down
Time complexity
Space complexity
Worst case is O(n) with bad luck; max level cap
Simpler code, lock-free concurrency, range scans: Redis, LevelDB, ConcurrentSkipListMap

questions.modelAnswer: A skip list is a sorted linked list with additional levels of sparser linked lists acting as express lanes. Every node is in level 0; each node is promoted to the next level with probability p (usually 1/2 or 1/4), so level i holds about n * p^i nodes. Search starts at the top-left, moves right while the next key is smaller than the target, and drops down a level when it would overshoot; at each level you expect only a constant number of steps, and there are about log(n) levels, so search is O(log n) expected. Insert finds the predecessors at each level during the search, draws a random height, and splices the new node into those lists; delete unlinks it at each level. No rotations or rebalancing are needed - randomness keeps the structure balanced in expectation, though the worst case is O(n) with astronomically bad luck; cap the maximum level at about log(n). Space is O(n) with on average 1/(1-p) pointers per node. Skip lists are much simpler to implement than red-black trees, support efficient ordered range scans, and are easy to make concurrent or lock-free because updates touch only local pointers - hence Redis sorted sets, LevelDB/RocksDB memtables and Java ConcurrentSkipListMap.

questions.title: B-trees and B+ trees
questions.prompt: Explain why databases and file systems use B-trees and B+ trees instead of binary search trees. Describe node structure and fan-out, how insertion splits nodes, the difference between B-trees and B+ trees, and the complexity in terms of disk or page reads.

expectedConcepts.label: Minimise page reads: wide nodes, shallow height
Node holds many sorted keys and child pointers
Insert into leaf; split full nodes and push middle key up
Time complexity
B+ tree: data only in leaves, leaves linked for range scans
Deletion merges/borrows; fill factor; random inserts fragment pages

questions.modelAnswer: Binary trees have height log2(n) and each step may be a random disk or memory page access - for a billion keys that is 30 reads. A B-tree node is sized to a page (4-16 KB) and holds hundreds of sorted keys with child pointers between them, so fan-out is in the hundreds and a billion keys fit in 3-4 levels, where the top levels are cached in memory. Search binary-searches within a node and follows one pointer per level: O(log_B n) page reads. Insert goes into the correct leaf; if it overflows, split it in two and push the middle key up into the parent, which may split recursively; when the root splits, the tree grows one level at the top, so all leaves stay at the same depth. Deletion borrows from or merges with siblings to keep nodes at least half full. In a B+ tree (used by most databases: InnoDB, PostgreSQL indexes, file systems), internal nodes hold only keys for routing and all records or row pointers live in the leaves, which are linked in order; this increases fan-out and makes range scans a sequential walk across leaves. Inserting random keys such as UUIDv4 causes page splits all over the tree and poor fill factor, which is why time-ordered keys are preferred.

questions.title: Bit manipulation tricks and when to use them
questions.prompt: Explain the core bit manipulation techniques: checking, setting and clearing bits, x & (x - 1), isolating the lowest set bit, XOR properties, and bitmasks for subsets. Use them to find the single non-duplicated number and count set bits, with complexities and pitfalls.

expectedConcepts.label: AND/OR/XOR/shift to test, set, clear, toggle bits
x & (x-1) clears lowest bit; x & -x isolates it; power of two test
XOR: a^a = 0, a^0 = a; single number
Time complexity
Space complexity
Pitfalls: signed shifts, overflow, operator precedence
Bitmask subsets, bitsets; hash set alternative

questions.modelAnswer: Test bit i with (x >> i) & 1, set it with x | (1 << i), clear it with x & ~(1 << i), and toggle it with x ^ (1 << i). x & (x - 1) clears the lowest set bit, so x is a power of two exactly when x > 0 and x & (x - 1) == 0, and repeatedly applying it counts set bits in O(number of set bits) (Kernighan); hardware popcount does it in one instruction. x & -x isolates the lowest set bit thanks to two's complement, which is how Fenwick trees navigate. XOR is associative and commutative with a ^ a = 0 and a ^ 0 = a, so XOR-ing every element of an array where all numbers appear twice except one leaves that single number: O(n) time, O(1) space, versus O(n) space for a hash set. Bitmasks represent subsets of up to ~20-30 items as integers: iterating mask from 0 to 2^n - 1 enumerates all subsets, and DP over masks solves TSP-style problems. Pitfalls: right-shifting negative numbers is arithmetic in many languages, 1 << 31 overflows a signed int, and & binds more loosely than == in C-like languages, so parenthesise.

questions.title: Coin change: minimum coins and number of ways
questions.prompt: Solve two coin change problems with dynamic programming: the minimum number of coins to make an amount, and the number of distinct ways to make it. Explain the states and recurrences, why the loop order matters for counting combinations versus permutations, and why greedy fails.

expectedConcepts.label: dp[a] = 1 + min(dp[a - coin])
ways[a] += ways[a - coin]
Coins outer loop = combinations; amount outer loop = permutations
Time complexity
Space complexity
Greedy fails for non-canonical coin systems
Base cases: dp[0] = 0, unreachable = infinity / -1

questions.modelAnswer: Minimum coins: dp[a] is the fewest coins summing to a. dp[0] = 0, everything else starts at infinity, and dp[a] = 1 + min over coins c <= a of dp[a - c]. If dp[amount] is still infinity, return -1. Time O(n * amount) for n coin types, space O(amount). Number of ways: ways[0] = 1 (one way to make zero - choose nothing) and ways[a] += ways[a - c]. Loop order matters: with coins in the outer loop and amounts in the inner loop, each coin is considered once in a fixed order, so {1,2} and {2,1} count as one combination; with amounts outer and coins inner you count ordered sequences (permutations), which answers a different question such as "number of ways to climb stairs with steps 1 and 2". Greedy (always take the largest coin) works for canonical systems like 1, 2, 5, 10 but fails for coins {1, 3, 4} and amount 6: greedy gives 4+1+1 (three coins) while 3+3 needs two. BFS over amounts is an alternative for the minimum. Watch for integer overflow in the counting version, so use modular arithmetic or big integers when asked.

questions.title: Counting paths in a grid with dynamic programming
questions.prompt: Count the number of paths from the top-left to the bottom-right of an m by n grid moving only right or down, then handle obstacles and a minimum-cost path. Explain the recurrence, the base cases, the complexity and how to reduce memory to one row.

expectedConcepts.label: paths[i][j] = paths[i-1][j] + paths[i][j-1]
First row and column have one path; obstacles are zero
Time complexity
Space complexity
Combinatorics C(m+n-2, m-1); recursion without memo is exponential

questions.modelAnswer: You can reach cell (i, j) only from the cell above or the cell to the left, so the number of paths is paths[i][j] = paths[i-1][j] + paths[i][j-1]. Every cell in the first row and first column has exactly one path. Fill the table row by row and return the bottom-right value: O(mn) time. Because each row only needs the previous row and the current row so far, a single array of length n works: for each row, dp[j] += dp[j-1]. With obstacles, set dp[j] = 0 at blocked cells, and if the start or end is blocked the answer is 0 - note that in the first row, cells after an obstacle are unreachable. For the minimum-cost path replace the sum with cost[i][j] + min(above, left). Without obstacles the count also has a closed form: choose which m-1 of the m+n-2 moves go down, C(m+n-2, m-1), but intermediate values overflow quickly. Naive recursion without memoisation recomputes subproblems and is exponential.

questions.title: Longest common subsequence
questions.prompt: Explain how to compute the longest common subsequence of two strings with dynamic programming. Define the state and recurrence, walk through how to reconstruct the subsequence itself, give complexities, and explain how LCS relates to diff tools and edit distance.

expectedConcepts.label: dp[i][j] = LCS of prefixes a[:i] and b[:j]
Match: 1 + diagonal; else max(up, left)
Time complexity
Space complexity
Reconstruct by walking back from dp[m][n]
Subsequence vs substring; diff tools; relation to edit distance

questions.modelAnswer: A subsequence keeps order but not contiguity: "ace" is a subsequence of "abcde". Let dp[i][j] be the LCS length of the first i characters of a and the first j of b, with dp[0][*] = dp[*][0] = 0. If a[i-1] == b[j-1], dp[i][j] = 1 + dp[i-1][j-1]; otherwise dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]), dropping a character from one string. Time and space O(mn). To reconstruct the sequence, start at (m, n): when the characters match, record it and move diagonally; otherwise move toward the larger neighbour; reverse the collected characters at the end. If only the length is needed, two rows suffice: O(min(m, n)) space, and Hirschberg's algorithm reconstructs in linear space. Edge cases: empty strings, identical strings, no common characters. Do not confuse it with longest common substring, which requires contiguity and resets to 0 on mismatch. diff tools show the lines not in the LCS as deletions and insertions, and edit distance with only insertions and deletions equals m + n - 2 * LCS; real diff tools use Myers' O(ND) algorithm, fast when files are similar.

questions.title: Interval dynamic programming
questions.prompt: Explain interval dynamic programming using matrix chain multiplication or burst balloons as the example. What is the state, why do you iterate by interval length, how do you choose the split point, and what is the complexity? How do you recognise an interval DP problem?

expectedConcepts.label: dp[i][j] = best answer for the interval i..j
Try every split k: dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j] + cost
Iterate by increasing length so subintervals are ready
Time complexity
Space complexity
Recognise: merging adjacent pieces, last action; Knuth optimisation

questions.modelAnswer: Interval DP solves problems where the answer for a contiguous range depends on how you split it. Matrix chain multiplication: dp[i][j] is the minimum scalar multiplications to compute the product of matrices i..j; for every split k between i and j-1, cost = dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j] + rows_i * cols_k * cols_j, and dp[i][j] is the minimum. Base case dp[i][i] = 0. Because dp[i][j] needs shorter intervals, fill the table by increasing interval length (or i descending, j ascending). There are O(n^2) states and O(n) choices each, so O(n^3) time and O(n^2) space. Burst balloons is the classic twist: instead of choosing the first balloon to burst, choose the last balloon k to burst in (i, j); then its neighbours at that moment are the fixed boundaries i and j, so dp[i][j] = max over k of dp[i][k] + dp[k][j] + nums[i] * nums[k] * nums[j], with padding 1s at both ends. Recognise interval DP when a choice in the middle splits the problem into independent left and right parts or when adjacent pieces are merged (merge stones, palindrome partitioning, optimal BST). Knuth's optimisation reduces some cases to O(n^2).

questions.title: Bitmask dynamic programming and the travelling salesman problem
questions.prompt: Explain bitmask dynamic programming using the travelling salesman problem on up to 20 cities. Define the state as a subset and a current city, give the transition and the complexity compared with brute force, and explain the practical limits and alternatives for larger inputs.

expectedConcepts.label: dp[mask][i] = min cost visiting set mask, ending at i
Transition: add an unvisited city j
Time complexity
Space complexity
Practical limit ~20 cities; memory; start city fixed
Heuristics and approximations: nearest neighbour, 2-opt, Christofides

questions.modelAnswer: Brute force over all tours is O(n!) - about 2.4 * 10^18 for 20 cities. Bitmask DP exploits the fact that the future only depends on which cities are visited and where you are, not the order. State: dp[mask][i] is the minimum cost of a path that starts at city 0, visits exactly the cities in mask, and ends at city i. Base: dp[1 << 0][0] = 0. Transition: for every state and every city j not in mask, dp[mask | (1 << j)][j] = min(current, dp[mask][i] + dist[i][j]). The answer is min over i of dp[all][i] + dist[i][0]. There are 2^n * n states and n transitions each: O(n^2 * 2^n) time - about 4 * 10^8 for n = 20 - and O(n * 2^n) memory, about 20 million entries, which is the practical ceiling. Store parents to reconstruct the tour. TSP is NP-hard, so beyond that use heuristics: nearest neighbour construction improved with 2-opt or Lin-Kernighan, Christofides' 1.5-approximation for metric distances, or integer programming solvers. The same bitmask technique solves assignment problems and "visit all nodes" shortest paths.

questions.title: Dynamic programming on trees
questions.prompt: Explain dynamic programming on trees using two examples: the maximum sum of non-adjacent nodes (house robber on a tree) and the diameter of a tree. Why does a post-order traversal fit, what does each node return, and what are the complexities and pitfalls?

expectedConcepts.label: Post-order: children computed before parent
Return a pair: best with node taken, best without
Diameter: at each node, left height + right height
Time complexity
Space complexity
Edge cases: skewed trees overflow the stack; global vs returned value
Memoisation by node is O(n) too; rerooting for all roots

questions.modelAnswer: Tree DP computes something for each subtree from its children's results, so a post-order DFS fits naturally. House robber on a tree: you cannot take a node and its parent together. Each call returns a pair (take, skip): take = node.val + skip(left) + skip(right), skip = max(take, skip) of left + max(take, skip) of right. The answer is max(take, skip) at the root. Each node is processed once, O(n) time, and returning both values avoids the exponential blow-up of naive recursion that recomputes grandchildren (memoising by node in a hash map also works but costs more). Diameter: each call returns the height of its subtree, and while doing so updates a global best with left height + right height, the longest path passing through that node. Both use O(h) recursion stack, which for a degenerate tree of a million nodes overflows the stack in many languages, so use an explicit stack. For questions like "for every node as the root, compute X" use rerooting: one DFS computes subtree answers, and a second pass pushes parent contributions down, keeping total O(n).

questions.title: Checking whether a graph is bipartite
questions.prompt: Explain how to check whether an undirected graph is bipartite using BFS or DFS two-colouring. Why is a graph bipartite exactly when it has no odd-length cycle, what are the complexity and edge cases, and where does bipartiteness appear in real problems?

expectedConcepts.label: Two-colour with BFS/DFS; neighbours get opposite colours
Conflict means an odd cycle
Time complexity
Space complexity
Disconnected components; self-loops
Union-find alternative; matching, scheduling applications

questions.modelAnswer: A graph is bipartite if its vertices can be split into two sets with every edge going between the sets. Check it by two-colouring: pick an uncoloured vertex, colour it 0, and BFS (or DFS); each neighbour gets the opposite colour, and if you ever find an edge whose endpoints have the same colour, the graph is not bipartite. Repeat from every uncoloured vertex, because the graph may be disconnected. Time O(V + E), space O(V). Correctness: walking along a cycle alternates colours, so an even cycle closes consistently while an odd cycle forces two adjacent vertices to share a colour; conversely, if BFS finds a conflict, the two BFS paths plus the conflicting edge form an odd cycle. So bipartite means no odd cycle. A self-loop makes a graph non-bipartite. Union-find also works: for each vertex, union all its neighbours together and check the vertex is never in the same set as a neighbour. Applications: splitting people into two teams with "dislikes" constraints, job-worker assignment and maximum bipartite matching, and detecting whether a scheduling conflict graph can use two time slots.

questions.title: Strongly connected components
questions.prompt: Explain strongly connected components in a directed graph and how Kosaraju's or Tarjan's algorithm finds them in linear time. What is the condensation graph, and where are SCCs used in practice, for example in dependency analysis or 2-SAT?

expectedConcepts.label: SCC: maximal set where every node reaches every other
Kosaraju: DFS finish order, then DFS on the reversed graph
Tarjan: one DFS with discovery index and low-link, stack
Time complexity
Space complexity
Condensation graph is a DAG
Uses: cyclic dependencies, 2-SAT, deadlock detection; recursion depth

questions.modelAnswer: In a directed graph, a strongly connected component is a maximal set of vertices where each can reach every other. Kosaraju: run DFS over the whole graph recording vertices in order of finishing; then reverse all edges and run DFS in decreasing finish time - each tree found in the second pass is exactly one SCC. It needs two passes and the transposed graph. Tarjan: a single DFS assigns each vertex a discovery index and a low-link value (the smallest index reachable via the DFS subtree plus one back edge to a vertex still on the stack); vertices are pushed onto a stack, and when a vertex's low-link equals its own index it is the root of an SCC, so pop the stack down to it. Both run in O(V + E) time and O(V) space. Contracting each SCC to a single node yields the condensation graph, which is always a DAG, so you can topologically sort it. Uses: finding circular dependency groups in build systems or package graphs, solving 2-SAT (a formula is satisfiable iff no variable and its negation share an SCC), deadlock detection in wait-for graphs, and simplifying graphs before other algorithms. Large graphs need iterative implementations to avoid stack overflow.

questions.title: Bridges and articulation points
questions.prompt: Explain how to find bridges and articulation points (cut vertices) in an undirected graph in linear time using DFS discovery times and low-link values. Why do these matter for network reliability, and what edge cases trip people up, such as the DFS root and parallel edges?

expectedConcepts.label: Bridge/cut vertex: removal disconnects the graph
Discovery time and low-link via back edges
Bridge if low[v] > disc[u]; cut vertex if low[v] >= disc[u]
Time complexity
Space complexity
Root is a cut vertex only with 2+ DFS children; parallel edges; skip parent edge
Brute force removes each edge: O(E(V+E)); reliability uses

questions.modelAnswer: A bridge is an edge whose removal disconnects the graph; an articulation point is a vertex whose removal does. Brute force removes each edge or vertex and re-checks connectivity, O(E(V + E)). Tarjan's DFS does it in one pass. Record disc[u], the time u was discovered, and low[u], the smallest discovery time reachable from u's DFS subtree using at most one back edge. For each tree edge u -> v after exploring v: low[u] = min(low[u], low[v]); for a back edge to an already visited w (other than the edge to the parent), low[u] = min(low[u], disc[w]). Edge (u, v) is a bridge if low[v] > disc[u]: nothing in v's subtree can reach u or above without that edge. A non-root u is an articulation point if some child v has low[v] >= disc[u]; the DFS root is one only if it has two or more DFS children. Time O(V + E), space O(V). Pitfalls: with parallel edges, skip the parent edge by edge id rather than by vertex, otherwise a doubled edge is wrongly reported as a bridge; and recursion depth on big graphs. In networks these are single points of failure; adding redundant links to make components biconnected removes them.

questions.title: Maximum flow and minimum cut
questions.prompt: Explain the maximum flow problem and the Ford-Fulkerson method with residual graphs and augmenting paths. Why does Edmonds-Karp use BFS, what does the max-flow min-cut theorem say, and how do you reduce bipartite matching to max flow?

expectedConcepts.label: Residual graph with reverse edges allows undoing flow
Repeatedly find augmenting paths and push bottleneck flow
Edmonds-Karp: BFS shortest augmenting paths, O(V E^2)
Space complexity
Max flow = min cut capacity
Dinic, bipartite matching reduction, applications

questions.modelAnswer: Given a directed graph with edge capacities, a source s and a sink t, maximum flow asks how much can be sent from s to t without exceeding capacities, with flow conserved at every other vertex. Ford-Fulkerson: keep a residual graph where each edge has remaining capacity, and for every unit of flow pushed along u -> v add residual capacity on v -> u so later paths can cancel earlier choices. While some s-t path exists in the residual graph (an augmenting path), push its bottleneck capacity along it. With DFS and irrational or huge capacities it can be slow or not terminate; Edmonds-Karp always picks the shortest augmenting path by BFS, giving O(V * E^2). Dinic's algorithm uses BFS level graphs and blocking flows, O(V^2 E) in general and much faster on unit-capacity graphs. Max-flow min-cut theorem: the maximum flow equals the minimum total capacity of edges whose removal separates s from t; after the algorithm finishes, the vertices reachable from s in the residual graph form one side of a minimum cut. Bipartite matching: add a super source to every left vertex and every right vertex to a super sink, all capacities 1; the max flow is the maximum matching. Applications: assigning jobs, network reliability, image segmentation.

questions.title: All-pairs shortest paths: Floyd-Warshall
questions.prompt: Explain the Floyd-Warshall algorithm for all-pairs shortest paths. Describe the dynamic programming idea behind the triple loop, why the intermediate vertex must be the outer loop, how it detects negative cycles, and when you would prefer running Dijkstra from every vertex instead.

expectedConcepts.label: dist[i][j] via intermediate vertices 1..k
k must be the outermost loop
Time complexity
Space complexity
Negative cycle if dist[i][i] < 0
Dijkstra from every vertex for sparse non-negative graphs; Johnson

questions.modelAnswer: Floyd-Warshall computes shortest distances between every pair of vertices. Initialise dist[i][j] to the edge weight (0 on the diagonal, infinity if no edge). Then for k from 1 to V, for every i and j: dist[i][j] = min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k] + dist[k][j]). The invariant is that after processing k, dist[i][j] is the shortest path using only vertices 1..k as intermediates; the next k either improves a path by routing through k or not. That is why k must be the outermost loop - putting it inside computes something else. Time O(V^3), space O(V^2), and it handles negative edge weights. If any dist[i][i] becomes negative, vertex i lies on a negative cycle and shortest paths through it are undefined. Keep a next[i][j] matrix to reconstruct paths. For sparse graphs with non-negative weights, running Dijkstra from every vertex costs O(V (V + E) log V), much better than V^3 when E is small; Johnson's algorithm reweights edges with Bellman-Ford to allow that even with negative edges. Floyd-Warshall shines for dense graphs, small V (a few hundred) and its very simple code; also for transitive closure with booleans.

questions.title: Grid problems: islands and multi-source BFS
questions.prompt: Explain how to count islands in a 2D grid and how to compute the minimum time for rot to spread to every orange using multi-source BFS. Describe treating a grid as an implicit graph, marking visited cells, the complexities, and when to choose BFS, DFS or union-find.

expectedConcepts.label: Grid as implicit graph with 4-directional neighbours
Flood fill each unvisited land cell; count launches
Multi-source BFS: start queue with all sources; levels = minutes
Time complexity
Space complexity
Edge cases: empty grid, unreachable fresh cells return -1, recursion depth
DFS vs BFS vs union-find (dynamic islands)

questions.modelAnswer: A grid is an implicit graph: each cell is a vertex connected to its up, down, left and right neighbours inside the bounds. Number of islands: scan every cell; when you find unvisited land, increment the count and flood-fill the whole island with BFS or DFS, marking cells as visited (or overwriting them with water if mutation is allowed). Every cell is visited a constant number of times, O(mn) time and O(mn) worst-case space for the queue or recursion - recursive DFS can overflow the stack on a huge all-land grid, so iterative BFS is safer. Rotting oranges: instead of one BFS per rotten orange, push all initially rotten cells into the queue at time 0 and run a single BFS level by level; each level is one minute, and fresh neighbours become rotten and join the next level. If fresh oranges remain afterwards, return -1. Multi-source BFS gives each cell its distance to the nearest source in O(mn), the same trick used for "distance to nearest gate". Union-find is better when land is added over time and you must report the island count after each addition.

questions.title: Word ladder: BFS for shortest transformations
questions.prompt: Find the length of the shortest transformation sequence from a begin word to an end word, changing one letter at a time, where every intermediate word must be in a dictionary. Explain why BFS is the right tool, how to generate neighbours efficiently, the complexity, and how bidirectional BFS helps.

expectedConcepts.label: Unweighted shortest path = BFS
Neighbours by changing each position to a-z, or wildcard patterns
Time complexity
Space complexity
End word missing from dictionary; mark visited when enqueued
Bidirectional BFS; comparing all pairs is O(N^2 L)

questions.modelAnswer: Treat each word as a vertex and connect words that differ in one letter. Every move costs 1, so the shortest sequence is a BFS shortest path from the begin word. Building the graph by comparing all pairs is O(N^2 * L). Instead generate neighbours on the fly: for each position replace the letter with a to z and check the dictionary hash set, O(26 * L) candidates each costing O(L) to build and hash; or precompute buckets keyed by wildcard patterns like h*t. Each word enters the queue once, so time is about O(N * L^2) (times 26 for the letter method) and space O(N * L). Remove words from the set or mark them visited when you enqueue them, not when you dequeue them, to avoid adding the same word many times. If the end word is not in the dictionary, the answer is 0. Bidirectional BFS searches from both ends, always expanding the smaller frontier, and stops when they meet; since the frontier grows exponentially with depth, this explores roughly two half-depth searches instead of one full-depth search - a large speedup. Returning all shortest paths requires recording parents per level.

questions.title: Reservoir sampling
questions.prompt: You need to choose k items uniformly at random from a stream of unknown length that is too large to store. Explain reservoir sampling, prove that every item ends up in the sample with probability k over n, and discuss weighted sampling and distributed variants.

expectedConcepts.label: Keep first k; for item i, replace a random slot with probability k/i
Induction: each item stays with probability k/n
Time complexity
Space complexity
Stream shorter than k; random number quality; off-by-one
Weighted (A-Res with keys u^(1/w)), distributed: random keys + top k, Algorithm L

questions.modelAnswer: Keep the first k items in a reservoir. For the i-th item (1-indexed, i > k), generate a random integer r in [1, i]; if r <= k, replace reservoir[r] with the new item. This uses one pass, O(n) time and O(k) memory, without knowing n in advance. Proof by induction: after processing i items, each has probability k/i of being in the reservoir. Item i+1 is inserted with probability k/(i+1). An item already in the reservoir survives step i+1 unless it is selected for replacement, which happens with probability (k/(i+1)) * (1/k) = 1/(i+1), so it remains with probability (k/i) * (i/(i+1)) = k/(i+1). Hence at the end every item is present with probability k/n. If the stream has fewer than k items, return them all. For weighted sampling, give each item the key u^(1/w) with u uniform in (0, 1) and keep the k largest keys in a min-heap (Efraimidis-Spirakis). This random-key formulation also parallelises: each machine keeps its top-k keys and you merge them. Algorithm L skips ahead geometrically so you do not need a random number for every item, which matters for very long streams.

questions.title: Sliding window maximum with a monotonic deque
questions.prompt: Given an array and a window size k, return the maximum of every window. Explain the monotonic deque solution, why it runs in O(n), what the deque stores and why indices rather than values, and compare it with a heap and with a block-based approach.

expectedConcepts.label: Deque of indices with decreasing values
Pop smaller from back; pop expired from front; front is max
Time complexity
Space complexity
Indices detect expiry; k = 1; k = n; duplicates
Heap with lazy deletion O(n log k); block prefix/suffix max

questions.modelAnswer: Keep a deque of indices whose values are in strictly decreasing order from front to back. For each new index i: pop indices from the back while their value is less than or equal to nums[i] - they can never be a maximum again because a larger, newer element covers them for as long as they would remain in the window; push i at the back; pop the front if it has fallen out of the window (index <= i - k). Once i >= k - 1, the front holds the maximum of the current window. Each index is pushed and popped at most once, so the total is O(n) amortised, and the deque holds at most k indices, O(k) space. Storing indices rather than values is what lets you detect expired elements, especially with duplicates. A max-heap of (value, index) with lazy removal of expired tops costs O(n log k). Another O(n) approach splits the array into blocks of size k and precomputes prefix maxima and suffix maxima within each block; any window spans at most two blocks, so its max is max(suffix[i], prefix[i + k - 1]). Edge cases: k = 1 returns the array, k = n returns one value.

questions.title: Top k frequent elements
questions.prompt: Return the k most frequent elements in an array. Compare sorting by frequency, a min-heap of size k, bucket sort by frequency and quickselect, with complexities. Then explain how you would approximate the top k over an unbounded stream with limited memory.

expectedConcepts.label: Count frequencies with a hash map
Min-heap of size k on frequency
Bucket sort: index by frequency, O(n)
Time complexity
Space complexity
Ties, k equal to distinct count, empty input
Streams: Count-Min Sketch + heap, Misra-Gries / Space-Saving

questions.modelAnswer: First count frequencies with a hash map in O(n). Then: sorting the distinct elements by count is O(m log m) for m distinct values. A min-heap of size k keyed by frequency - push each element and pop when the heap exceeds k - gives O(m log k), good when k is small. Bucket sort is O(n): frequencies range from 1 to n, so create an array of n + 1 lists, put each element in the bucket of its frequency, and walk from the highest bucket down collecting k elements. Quickselect on frequencies gives O(m) average. Space is O(n) for the counts. Clarify tie-breaking (any order, or by value) and handle k equal to the number of distinct elements. For an unbounded stream you cannot keep exact counts for every key. Count-Min Sketch keeps a small 2D array of counters updated by several hash functions, over-estimating counts by a bounded error, combined with a heap of current top candidates; Misra-Gries or Space-Saving keep k counters and guarantee to find every element with frequency above n/k. These heavy-hitter algorithms power trending topics and network traffic monitoring.

questions.title: Analysing recursive algorithms and the master theorem
questions.prompt: Explain how to analyse the running time of recursive algorithms. Write recurrences for binary search, mergesort and naive Fibonacci, solve them with recursion trees, state the master theorem and its three cases, and give an example where the master theorem does not apply.

expectedConcepts.label: Recurrence T(n) = a T(n/b) + f(n)
keywords: a t of n over b

expectedConcepts.label: Recursion tree: work per level times number of levels
Master theorem: compare f(n) with n^(log_b a)
Examples: binary search log n, mergesort n log n, Fibonacci exponential
Space complexity
Not applicable: T(n) = T(n-1) + n, uneven splits, non-polynomial gaps

questions.modelAnswer: A recursive algorithm's cost is a recurrence. Binary search makes one call on half the input plus constant work: T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) = O(log n). Mergesort makes two calls on halves plus a linear merge: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n); the recursion tree has log n levels each doing n work, so O(n log n). Naive Fibonacci T(n) = T(n-1) + T(n-2) + O(1) grows like phi^n (about 1.618^n), which is why memoisation turning it into O(n) matters. The master theorem solves T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n) with a >= 1, b > 1 by comparing f(n) to n^(log_b a), the total work at the leaves: (1) if f(n) is polynomially smaller, the leaves dominate and T = Theta(n^(log_b a)) - e.g. Karatsuba, 3T(n/2) + n = n^1.585; (2) if they are equal up to log factors, T = Theta(n^(log_b a) log n) - mergesort; (3) if f(n) is polynomially larger (with a regularity condition), the root dominates and T = Theta(f(n)). It does not apply to subtract-and-conquer recurrences like T(n) = T(n-1) + n (which is O(n^2)), uneven splits like T(n/3) + T(2n/3) + n (use a recursion tree or Akra-Bazzi), or gaps that are only logarithmic in some versions. Space is bounded by the recursion depth times the work per frame.

questions.title: Palindrome problems: expand around centre and Manacher
questions.prompt: Find the longest palindromic substring of a string. Explain the brute-force approach, the dynamic programming table, the expand-around-centre method and why there are 2n - 1 centres, and summarise how Manacher's algorithm achieves linear time. Contrast it with the longest palindromic subsequence.

expectedConcepts.label: Expand around each of 2n-1 centres (odd and even)
DP: dp[i][j] true if ends match and inside is palindrome
Time complexity
Space complexity
Manacher reuses mirror information for O(n)
Even-length palindromes, single char, substring vs subsequence

questions.modelAnswer: Brute force checks every substring for being a palindrome: O(n^2) substrings times O(n) checks = O(n^3). DP: dp[i][j] is true if s[i] == s[j] and dp[i+1][j-1] is true (or the length is at most 2); filling by increasing length gives O(n^2) time and O(n^2) space. Expand around centre: every palindrome mirrors around a centre, which is either a character (odd length) or a gap between two characters (even length) - 2n - 1 centres in total. From each, expand outwards while the characters match and track the longest; O(n^2) worst case (for "aaaa...") but O(1) extra space and very fast in practice. Forgetting the even-length centres is the most common bug. Manacher's algorithm reaches O(n): it transforms the string with separators so all palindromes are odd, keeps the rightmost palindrome boundary found so far, and initialises each new centre's radius from its mirror inside that palindrome, only expanding beyond the boundary, so total expansion work is linear. The longest palindromic subsequence (not contiguous) is a different problem: it equals the LCS of the string and its reverse, O(n^2).

questions.title: NP-completeness for software engineers
questions.prompt: Explain P, NP, NP-complete and NP-hard in practical terms. What is a polynomial-time reduction, how would you recognise that a problem you face at work is NP-hard, and what do engineers actually do then: approximation, heuristics, exponential algorithms on small inputs, or solvers?

expectedConcepts.label: P solvable fast; NP verifiable fast; NP-complete hardest in NP
Reduction maps a known hard problem to yours
Examples: SAT, TSP, knapsack, graph colouring, scheduling
Time complexity
Approximation, heuristics, small-n exact, special structure, SAT/ILP solvers
Pseudo-polynomial DP, average vs worst case, P vs NP open

questions.modelAnswer: P is the class of decision problems solvable in polynomial time. NP is the class whose "yes" answers can be verified in polynomial time given a certificate - a proposed schedule or assignment can be checked quickly even if finding one seems hard. A problem is NP-hard if every NP problem reduces to it in polynomial time, and NP-complete if it is both NP-hard and in NP. A reduction transforms instances of a known hard problem into instances of yours, so a fast algorithm for yours would solve the hard one - proving yours is at least as hard. Classic NP-complete problems: SAT, 3-colouring, vertex cover, subset sum, decision versions of TSP and 0/1 knapsack, many scheduling and bin-packing problems. Whether P = NP is open, but nobody expects a polynomial algorithm. Recognising it at work: your problem looks like "choose a subset or ordering subject to constraints to optimise something" and maps onto one of these. Then: exploit special structure (trees, planar graphs, small parameters), use pseudo-polynomial DP when numbers are small (knapsack is O(nW)), solve small instances exactly with bitmask DP or branch and bound, use approximation algorithms with guarantees, local-search heuristics, or hand it to mature SAT, constraint or integer-programming solvers, which handle large real-world instances surprisingly well because worst cases are rare.

questions.title: Modular arithmetic, GCD and fast exponentiation
questions.prompt: Explain the number-theory tools that appear in coding interviews: Euclid's GCD algorithm, fast modular exponentiation by squaring, why answers are often taken modulo 1e9+7, and how to divide under a modulus using a modular inverse. Give complexities and overflow pitfalls.

expectedConcepts.label: Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b)
Exponentiation by squaring
Mod keeps numbers small; 1e9+7 is prime
Time complexity
Space complexity
Modular inverse via Fermat's little theorem or extended Euclid
Overflow in multiplication, negative mod results, inverse needs coprime

questions.modelAnswer: Euclid's algorithm computes gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b) until b is 0; the numbers shrink at least by half every two steps, so it is O(log min(a, b)). lcm(a, b) = a / gcd(a, b) * b (divide first to avoid overflow). Fast exponentiation computes a^n by squaring: if n is even, a^n = (a^(n/2))^2; if odd, multiply by a once more - iteratively, walk the bits of n, squaring the base each step. That is O(log n) multiplications instead of n. Counting problems produce astronomically large answers, so they ask for the result modulo a large prime like 1,000,000,007: it fits in 32 bits, the product of two residues fits in 64 bits, and because it is prime every non-zero number has a multiplicative inverse. Addition, subtraction and multiplication commute with mod, but division does not; instead multiply by the modular inverse. By Fermat's little theorem, for prime p, a^(p-2) mod p is the inverse of a; the extended Euclidean algorithm finds inverses for any modulus coprime to a. Pitfalls: multiplying two values near 1e9 overflows 32-bit integers, in C++ and Java a negative number mod p is negative (add p), and an inverse does not exist when gcd(a, m) is not 1.

questions.title: Scaling a web app from one server to millions of users
questions.prompt: Walk through how a web application evolves from a single server to serving millions of users. Explain each step - separating the database, adding a load balancer and stateless app servers, caching, a CDN, read replicas, queues and sharding - and what problem each step solves.

expectedConcepts.label: Requirements and scale estimates
Separate DB; stateless app servers behind a load balancer
Move sessions out of app servers (Redis/cookies)
Caching and CDN for static content
Read replicas, then sharding for writes
Queues for slow background work
Find the bottleneck with monitoring before scaling
Trade-offs: complexity, consistency (replica lag), cost

questions.modelAnswer: Start: one server runs the web app and database - simple but a single point of failure, and both compete for CPU and memory. Step 1: move the database to its own machine so each can be sized independently. Step 2: run several app servers behind a load balancer; this requires stateless servers, so store sessions in a shared store such as Redis or in signed cookies instead of server memory. Now you can add servers and survive one dying. Step 3: add a cache (Redis/Memcached) for hot reads and a CDN for images, scripts and other static assets, which removes most traffic from the origin. Step 4: the database becomes the bottleneck; add read replicas for read-heavy workloads, accepting replication lag. Step 5: move slow work (emails, image processing) onto queues processed by workers so requests stay fast. Step 6: when writes outgrow one primary, shard data by a key such as user id, and split the system into services along team or domain boundaries. Throughout, add monitoring and scale the actual bottleneck. Each step adds operational complexity and new consistency problems, so do not jump ahead of real need.

questions.title: Back-of-the-envelope capacity estimation
questions.prompt: In a system design interview you are asked to estimate the storage, bandwidth and server count for a photo-sharing app with 100 million daily active users. Walk through how you make and state assumptions, convert daily volumes to per-second rates and peak, and use the numbers to drive design decisions.

expectedConcepts.label: Requirements and scale estimates
Convert per day to per second (~1e5 s/day) and apply peak factor
Storage = writes x size x retention x replication
Bandwidth for reads dominates; CDN
Servers = peak QPS / per-server capacity, plus headroom
Numbers drive choices: caching, sharding, object storage
Round numbers, state uncertainty, order of magnitude is enough

questions.modelAnswer: State assumptions out loud and round aggressively: 100M daily active users; 10% post one photo a day = 10M uploads/day; each user views 50 photos = 5B views/day. A day is about 86,400 seconds, call it 1e5: uploads are ~100/s and views ~50,000/s on average; with a 3-5x peak factor, plan for ~500 uploads/s and ~200,000 views/s. Storage: 10M photos x 2 MB average (plus a few resized versions, say 3 MB total) = 30 TB/day, ~11 PB/year before replication, so photos must live in object storage, not a database, and old photos should move to cheaper tiers. Metadata: 10M rows/day x 1 KB = 10 GB/day, fine for a sharded database. Bandwidth: 200,000 views/s x 200 KB thumbnails = 40 GB/s egress - impossible from origin, so a CDN is mandatory and cache hit ratio is a key metric. Servers: if one app server handles ~2,000 simple requests/s, metadata reads need about 100 servers at peak plus headroom and redundancy across zones. The point is not precision but to find the dominant costs (here egress and storage) and let them drive the design; sanity-check results against known systems.

questions.title: Design a pastebin service
questions.prompt: Design a service like Pastebin where users paste text and get a short link to share it, with optional expiry. Cover requirements, the API, where to store paste content versus metadata, key generation, expiry and cleanup, caching and abuse prevention.

expectedConcepts.label: Requirements and scale estimates
API: create paste, get paste
Content in object storage, metadata in DB
Random or counter-based short keys
Expiry via TTL and background cleanup
Cache popular pastes; CDN
Rate limiting and content scanning
Trade-offs: guessable keys vs privacy, storage cost

questions.modelAnswer: Requirements: create a paste (up to, say, 10 MB of text), get a unique short URL, view it, optional expiry and private/unlisted pastes; reads outnumber writes about 10:1; for 1M new pastes a day averaging 10 KB, storage grows about 10 GB/day. API: POST /pastes returns {key, url}; GET /pastes/{key} returns content. Generate keys randomly (8 base62 characters is about 2 * 10^14 values, so collisions are rare and are checked on insert) or from pre-allocated counter ranges; random keys are better here because unlisted pastes should not be guessable. Store content in object storage keyed by the paste key and keep small metadata (key, owner, created, expires_at, size, visibility) in a database. Reads go through a cache or CDN for popular pastes. Expiry: check expires_at on read (lazy deletion) and run a periodic job that deletes expired metadata and objects, or use object-storage lifecycle rules. Abuse: rate-limit creation per IP/account, cap sizes, scan for malware and leaked credentials. Trade-off: keeping content in object storage is cheap and scales, at the cost of an extra hop that the cache hides.

questions.title: Design a full-text search system
questions.prompt: Design full-text search over a billion documents, such as product listings or posts. Explain the inverted index, tokenisation, how documents are indexed and kept fresh, how the index is sharded and replicated, how queries are scattered and gathered, and how results are ranked.

expectedConcepts.label: Requirements and scale estimates
Inverted index: term -> posting list
Indexing pipeline from change events; segments merged
Shard by document; scatter-gather queries
Ranking: BM25 then learned re-ranking
Replicas for availability and read throughput
Tail latency from slowest shard; hot queries
Near-real-time: index lag; deletes
Trade-offs: freshness vs indexing cost, recall vs latency

questions.modelAnswer: Requirements: keyword search with filters over 1B documents, p99 under 200 ms, new documents searchable within seconds, thousands of queries per second. Core structure: an inverted index mapping each term to a posting list of document ids (with term frequencies and positions), compressed and sorted so lists can be intersected quickly. Text goes through analysis - tokenisation, lowercasing, stemming, stop words, synonyms - identically at index and query time. Indexing: the source database emits change events (CDC) into a queue; indexers build small immutable segments that become searchable after a short refresh interval and are merged in the background, Lucene-style; deletes are tombstones until merges. Scale: shard by document id into, say, 100 shards of 10M docs, each replicated 2-3 times. A query goes to a coordinator that scatters it to one replica of each shard; each shard returns its top-k with scores (BM25), the coordinator merges them, then a second-stage learned model re-ranks the top few hundred. Tail latency is dominated by the slowest shard, so use replicas, hedged requests and timeouts with partial results; cache popular queries. Consistency is eventual: a just-updated document may show stale text briefly. Trade-offs: more shards parallelise but increase fan-out overhead.

questions.title: Design an e-commerce order system with sagas
questions.prompt: Design the order placement flow for an e-commerce platform where orders, inventory, payments and shipping are separate services with their own databases. Explain why distributed transactions are avoided, how a saga with compensating actions works, orchestration versus choreography, and how you handle failures midway.

expectedConcepts.label: Requirements and scale estimates
Avoid 2PC across services: blocking, coupling
Saga: sequence of local transactions with compensations
Orchestration vs choreography
Transactional outbox, idempotent consumers, retries
Order state machine with intermediate states
Hot inventory items, slow payment provider
Trade-offs: eventual consistency and visible intermediate states

questions.modelAnswer: Requirements: place an order, reserve stock, charge the customer, create a shipment; never oversell or charge for an order that cannot ship; services own their data. A two-phase commit across services would couple their availability, hold locks while waiting on a coordinator and is often unsupported by modern databases and brokers, so we use a saga: a sequence of local transactions, each publishing an event, with a compensating action for each step. Flow: Order service creates the order as PENDING; Inventory reserves items (compensation: release); Payment charges (compensation: refund); Shipping creates the shipment; finally the order becomes CONFIRMED. If payment fails, the saga runs compensations in reverse: release the stock and mark the order CANCELLED. Orchestration puts the flow in a central coordinator (a workflow engine such as Temporal or a state machine in the order service) - easy to see and change; choreography lets each service react to others' events - looser coupling but the flow is implicit and hard to follow. Reliability: every step is published via a transactional outbox, consumed at least once, and made idempotent with message ids; timeouts trigger retries or compensation. Saga steps lack isolation, so other readers see PENDING states; use semantic locks (reserved stock) and design the UI around them.

questions.title: Design a distributed log like Kafka
questions.prompt: Design a distributed, durable message log like Apache Kafka. Explain topics and partitions, how producers append and consumers track offsets, replication with leaders and in-sync replicas, ordering guarantees, consumer groups and rebalancing, retention, and delivery semantics.

expectedConcepts.label: Requirements and scale estimates
Append-only partitioned log; sequential disk I/O
Consumers pull and track offsets
Leader/follower replication, ISR, acks=all
Consumer groups: one consumer per partition; rebalancing
Ordering only within a partition; key-based partitioning
At-least-once by default; idempotent producer and transactions
Hot partitions, slow consumers, rebalance storms
Trade-offs: durability vs latency (acks), partitions vs overhead

questions.modelAnswer: Requirements: millions of messages per second, durable storage for days, replay, ordering per key, horizontal scale. A topic is split into partitions; each partition is an append-only log stored as segment files, written and read sequentially so throughput is limited by disk and network bandwidth rather than seeks, with the OS page cache and zero-copy sendfile serving consumers. Producers choose a partition by hashing a key, so all events for one key stay ordered; there is no ordering across partitions. Consumers pull batches and track their position as an offset, committing it periodically - so they can replay from any retained offset. Each partition has a leader and followers on other brokers; followers fetch from the leader, and the in-sync replica set (ISR) contains those caught up. With acks=all and min.insync.replicas=2, a write is acknowledged only once replicated, surviving a broker loss; if the leader dies, a controller (KRaft/Raft) promotes an in-sync follower. Consumer groups assign each partition to exactly one consumer in the group, so parallelism is capped by partition count, and membership changes trigger rebalancing. Delivery is at-least-once (commit after processing); idempotent producers and transactions give exactly-once within Kafka pipelines. Retention deletes old segments by time or size, or compacts to the latest value per key.

questions.title: Design a Dynamo-style distributed key-value store
questions.prompt: Design a highly available distributed key-value store like Amazon Dynamo or Cassandra. Explain partitioning with consistent hashing, replication, tunable consistency with quorums, conflict resolution, hinted handoff, anti-entropy with Merkle trees, and failure detection with gossip.

expectedConcepts.label: Requirements and scale estimates
Consistent hashing with virtual nodes
Replication factor N, quorum R + W > N
Conflict resolution: last-write-wins vs vector clocks
Sloppy quorum and hinted handoff
Anti-entropy with Merkle trees, read repair
Gossip membership and failure detection
Storage engine: LSM tree
Trade-offs: AP vs CP, stale reads, conflict complexity

questions.modelAnswer: Goal: a store that always accepts writes and serves reads with single-digit-millisecond latency even during node or network failures, accepting eventual consistency. Keys are partitioned with consistent hashing on a ring with virtual nodes, and each key is stored on the next N distinct nodes clockwise (its preference list). Any node can coordinate a request. Consistency is tunable with quorums: a write succeeds after W replicas acknowledge, a read waits for R replicas; R + W > N (e.g. N=3, R=2, W=2) means read and write sets overlap, so reads normally see the latest acknowledged write, while R=W=1 maximises availability and speed. Concurrent writes on different replicas create conflicts: Cassandra uses timestamps and last-write-wins (simple, can lose updates), Dynamo used vector clocks and returned siblings for the client to merge; CRDTs merge automatically. If a preferred replica is down, a sloppy quorum writes to another node with a hint and hands it off when the replica returns. Replicas drift, so anti-entropy compares Merkle trees of key ranges to sync only differing ranges, and read repair fixes stale replicas seen during reads. Membership and failures spread by gossip with accrual failure detectors. Each node stores data in an LSM tree for fast writes. Trade-off: availability over strong consistency (AP).

questions.title: Design a file sync service like Dropbox
questions.prompt: Design a file storage and sync service where users edit files on several devices and changes sync everywhere. Cover chunking and deduplication, the metadata service, upload and download flows, notifying devices of changes, conflict handling when two devices edit offline, and bandwidth efficiency.

expectedConcepts.label: Requirements and scale estimates
Split files into chunks, content-addressed by hash
Dedup and delta sync: upload only changed chunks
Metadata service: file versions -> chunk lists
Change notification via long polling/WebSockets and cursors
Conflicts: version check, conflicted copy
Durable object storage, resumable uploads
Metadata hot spots, large folders, many small files
Trade-offs: chunk size, client complexity, privacy vs dedup

questions.modelAnswer: Requirements: files up to tens of GB, many devices per user, offline edits, fast sync of small changes, no data loss, version history. The client splits files into chunks (fixed 4 MB, or content-defined chunking so an insertion does not shift every boundary) and hashes each one. The file is represented by an ordered list of chunk hashes. Upload: the client asks the metadata service which hashes are missing, uploads only those to object storage (resumable, with pre-signed URLs), then commits a new file version that references the chunk list, conditioned on the version it started from. Unchanged chunks are never re-sent, and identical chunks are stored once (deduplication). The metadata service is a strongly consistent, sharded database keyed by user or namespace, with an append-only journal of changes. Other devices hold a cursor into that journal and are notified via long polling or WebSockets; they fetch the changed metadata and download only missing chunks. Conflicts: if a device commits against an old base version, the server rejects it; the client keeps both and creates a "conflicted copy" rather than silently losing work. Bottlenecks: millions of tiny files (batch metadata operations), huge shared folders. Trade-off: cross-user deduplication saves storage but conflicts with client-side encryption and can leak information.

questions.title: Design a photo-sharing service like Instagram
questions.prompt: Design the core of a photo-sharing app: uploading photos, generating thumbnails, viewing a profile and a feed of followed users, likes and comments. Focus on storage choices for media and metadata, the upload pipeline, read scaling with caches and CDNs, and how counts like likes are kept.

expectedConcepts.label: Requirements and scale estimates
Direct upload to object storage via pre-signed URL; async processing
Workers generate thumbnails/variants
Metadata in sharded DB by user id
CDN serves images; caches for metadata
Like counts via counters / batched aggregation
Retries and idempotent processing
Celebrity posts, hot photos
Trade-offs: storage of variants vs on-the-fly resizing

questions.modelAnswer: Requirements: upload photos with captions, view profiles and a home feed, like and comment; very read-heavy; images must load fast globally. Upload: the client requests a pre-signed URL and uploads the original directly to object storage, then calls the API to create the post. A queue triggers workers that strip metadata such as GPS, generate thumbnails and several sizes and formats (WebP/AVIF), and mark the post ready. Metadata - users, posts, follows, comments - lives in databases sharded by user id (or post id for comments), with caches for hot profiles and posts. Images are served via a CDN using immutable, versioned URLs, so they can be cached forever. The feed uses the hybrid fan-out approach from news feed design. Likes: writing a row per like plus incrementing a counter on a hot post causes contention, so record likes in an append-only store and maintain counts with sharded counters or by aggregating like events in a stream processor every few seconds; the displayed count is eventually consistent, but whether "I liked it" must be read-your-writes. Processing is idempotent and retried. Trade-off: precomputing image variants costs storage but makes reads cheap; resizing on demand at the CDN edge saves storage at the cost of compute and first-hit latency.

questions.title: Design a real-time game leaderboard
questions.prompt: Design a leaderboard for an online game with 50 million players where scores update constantly and players want their rank, the top 100, and the players around them. Explain why a SQL ORDER BY does not scale, how Redis sorted sets work, sharding for very large boards, and time-windowed leaderboards.

expectedConcepts.label: Requirements and scale estimates
COUNT(*) WHERE score > x is O(n) per rank query
Redis sorted set: skip list, O(log n) update and rank
Top N and neighbours via ZREVRANGE
Sharding by score range or approximate global rank
Daily/weekly boards with keys per period and expiry
Persistence: Redis replication, rebuild from DB/event log
Ties and cheating validation
Trade-offs: exact vs approximate rank at large scale

questions.modelAnswer: Requirements: 50M players, thousands of score updates per second, top 100 in milliseconds, a player's exact rank and the 10 players around them. In SQL, finding a rank is SELECT COUNT(*) FROM scores WHERE score > :mine - a scan or large index range per request that does not scale under constant updates. Redis sorted sets keep members ordered by score using a skip list plus hash map: ZADD (or ZINCRBY) updates in O(log n), ZREVRANK returns a rank in O(log n), and ZREVRANGE returns the top 100 or a window around a rank. Fifty million entries is a few GB of memory - one large instance with replicas. Beyond that, shard: partition by score range so a player's global rank is the sum of counts in higher shards plus their rank within the shard, or give approximate ranks from a score histogram (top 1%). Time-windowed boards use one key per period (leaderboard:2026-10-19) with an expiry. Redis is not the source of truth: scores are written to a database or event log and the sorted set can be rebuilt. Ties need a deterministic rule, such as encoding an earlier timestamp into the score. Scores must be validated server-side against cheating. Trade-off: exact global rank is costly at extreme scale, and most players accept approximate percentiles.

questions.title: Design a nearby places service like Yelp
questions.prompt: Design a service that returns businesses within a given radius of a user, sorted by distance or rating, for 200 million businesses and heavy read traffic. Compare geohash, quadtree and S2 or H3 cells, explain the search algorithm including edges of cells, and how you handle updates and caching.

expectedConcepts.label: Requirements and scale estimates
Naive lat/long range query is inefficient
Geohash prefixes; neighbour cells for edges
Quadtree splits dense areas
S2/H3 cell coverings
Business data changes rarely: rebuild index, replicas
Cache by cell id
Stale results acceptable briefly; exact distance filter
Trade-offs: precision vs number of cells, density variation

questions.modelAnswer: Requirements: given a location and radius (500 m - 20 km) return nearby businesses ranked by distance or rating; 200M businesses; maybe 5,000 searches/s; business data changes rarely, so this is extremely read-heavy. A naive query WHERE lat BETWEEN ... AND lng BETWEEN ... can only use one dimension of a normal index efficiently. Geospatial indexing maps 2D space to 1D keys. Geohash encodes a location as a base32 string where a shared prefix means nearby; choose a precision whose cell size matches the radius and query the user's cell plus its 8 neighbours, because a nearby business can sit just across a cell boundary. A quadtree recursively splits regions until each leaf holds at most, say, 100 businesses, adapting to density (Manhattan versus desert); it is built in memory on each server. Google S2 and Uber H3 provide hierarchical cells and compute a covering of a circle with a few cells. After fetching candidates, compute exact distances (haversine), filter by radius and rank. Since data rarely changes, rebuild indexes periodically and serve from many read replicas or in-memory copies; cache results by cell id for popular areas. A new business appearing a few minutes late is acceptable. Trade-off: finer cells give fewer false candidates but more cells per query.

questions.title: Design a centralised logging pipeline
questions.prompt: Design a logging platform that collects logs from 10,000 services, makes them searchable within seconds, and retains them for months. Cover agents and buffering, the transport, indexing versus cheap storage, structured logs, sampling, cost control, multi-tenancy and protecting sensitive data.

expectedConcepts.label: Requirements and scale estimates
Agents tail and batch logs; local disk buffer
Kafka buffer between producers and indexers
Hot searchable index vs cheap object storage
Structured JSON logs with trace ids
Sampling, rate limits, retention per tenant
Redact secrets and PII; access control
Trade-offs: full-text index cost vs label-only (Loki style)

questions.modelAnswer: Requirements: maybe 5 GB/s of logs at peak from 10,000 services, searchable within about 10 seconds, 7-14 days hot and months cold, never block applications. Applications write structured JSON logs (timestamp, service, level, message, trace id, request id) to stdout; a node agent (Fluent Bit, Vector) tails them, adds metadata like pod and region, batches and compresses, and buffers to local disk if downstream is slow, dropping debug logs first rather than blocking the app. Agents ship to Kafka, which absorbs spikes and lets several consumers process the same stream. Indexers consume from Kafka and write to a search cluster (Elasticsearch/OpenSearch) partitioned by time and tenant for recent data; older data is rolled to compressed files in object storage, queryable more slowly. A cheaper design (Loki-style) indexes only labels and greps compressed chunks, trading query speed for far lower cost. Cost control: per-team quotas and rate limits, sampling of high-volume info logs, shorter retention for noisy services, and dashboards of top log producers. Security: redact secrets and personal data at the agent, enforce per-team access control, and audit log access. Correlating logs with traces via trace ids makes debugging fast.

questions.title: Design a feature flag and remote config service
questions.prompt: Design a feature flag service used by hundreds of services and mobile apps to turn features on gradually. Explain how flags are evaluated, why evaluation should be local, how updates propagate quickly, percentage rollouts with consistent bucketing, targeting rules, safety defaults and cleaning up old flags.

expectedConcepts.label: Requirements and scale estimates
SDKs evaluate locally from a cached ruleset
Updates via streaming/polling, CDN-distributed config
Consistent hashing of user id for percentage rollouts
Safe defaults when the service is down
Audit log, approvals, kill switches
Flag debt: expiry and cleanup
Trade-offs: propagation speed vs load, client-side exposure

questions.modelAnswer: Requirements: create flags with targeting rules (user attributes, regions, percentages), evaluate them millions of times per second with no added latency, propagate changes within seconds, and never take down callers. Architecture: an admin UI and API write flag definitions to a database with versioning and an audit log. SDKs inside each service download the full ruleset and evaluate flags locally in memory - a remote call per evaluation would add latency and a single point of failure. Updates propagate by streaming (server-sent events or WebSockets) from relay servers, with polling as a fallback; for mobile and browsers, rulesets can be cached on a CDN. Percentage rollouts must be sticky: hash(flag key + user id) mod 100 puts each user in a stable bucket, so increasing from 10% to 20% keeps the original 10% and adds more, and different flags bucket independently. Safety: every flag has a coded default used if the SDK has never loaded rules, and SDKs persist the last known ruleset. Kill switches let on-call disable a feature instantly; changes to production flags may need approval. Flags accumulate as technical debt, so give them owners and expiry dates and alert on flags fully rolled out for weeks. Trade-off: client-side flags expose rules to users, so keep secrets server-side.

questions.title: Design an ad click aggregation system
questions.prompt: Design a system that counts ad clicks in real time for billing and dashboards: one billion clicks a day, aggregated per ad per minute, with results needed within a minute and correctness required for billing. Explain stream processing, windowing, late events, exactly-once counting, deduplication and reconciliation.

expectedConcepts.label: Requirements and scale estimates
Click log into Kafka, raw events kept
Stream processor aggregates per ad per minute
Event time, watermarks, late events
Exactly-once via checkpoints and idempotent sinks; dedupe click ids
Batch reconciliation over raw data
Hot ads: pre-aggregate, key salting
Partition by ad id; scale with partitions
Trade-offs: latency vs completeness of windows

questions.modelAnswer: Requirements: 1B clicks/day (~12k/s average, 50k/s peak), per-ad per-minute counts available within a minute, plus fraud filtering; billing must be correct. Click servers validate and write raw events, each with a unique click id, to Kafka partitioned by ad id; raw events are also archived to object storage as the source of truth. A stream processor (Flink) reads them, deduplicates by click id within a time window, filters bots, and aggregates counts in one-minute tumbling windows based on event time - when the click happened - not processing time. Events arrive late and out of order (mobile devices offline), so watermarks decide when a window is complete enough to emit, with allowed lateness that later emits corrections. Exactly-once results come from checkpointing operator state together with Kafka offsets and writing results to an idempotent sink (upsert keyed by ad id + window). Hot ads would overload one partition, so pre-aggregate locally before the shuffle or salt keys and merge. Results go to an OLAP store for dashboards. For billing, a daily batch job recomputes counts from the raw archive and reconciles with the streaming totals; discrepancies are investigated. Trade-off: waiting longer for late events improves completeness but delays results.

questions.title: Design a content delivery network
questions.prompt: Design a content delivery network. Explain how users are routed to a nearby edge (DNS-based and anycast), the cache hierarchy with edge, regional and origin shield layers, cache keys and TTLs, invalidation, handling cache misses for popular content, TLS at the edge, and protection against attacks.

expectedConcepts.label: Requirements and scale estimates
Routing to nearest PoP: GeoDNS or anycast
Edge -> regional -> origin shield hierarchy
Cache keys, TTLs, Cache-Control, Vary
Purge/invalidation and versioned URLs
Request coalescing on miss
TLS termination, DDoS absorption, WAF
Trade-offs: freshness vs hit ratio, storage per PoP

questions.modelAnswer: Requirements: serve static and cacheable dynamic content to users worldwide with low latency, offload origin servers, and survive traffic spikes and attacks. Hundreds of points of presence (PoPs) sit near users. Routing: GeoDNS returns the IP of a nearby healthy PoP based on the resolver's location, or anycast advertises the same IP from every PoP so BGP routes users to the nearest one - anycast also spreads DDoS traffic. Inside a PoP, a load balancer hashes the URL to a cache server so each object is stored once per PoP. Cache hierarchy: on a miss, the edge asks a regional tier, which asks an origin shield, so the origin sees one request instead of one per PoP. The cache key is normally host + path + selected query parameters and Vary headers; TTLs come from Cache-Control. Request coalescing makes concurrent misses for the same object wait for a single origin fetch. Freshness: versioned or hashed asset URLs cached for a year are best; otherwise purge APIs propagate invalidations to all PoPs within seconds, and stale-while-revalidate serves old content while refreshing. The edge terminates TLS with managed certificates, applies WAF rules and rate limits, and absorbs volumetric attacks. Trade-off: long TTLs raise hit ratio but risk staleness; PoP storage is finite, so the long tail is evicted.

questions.title: Designing a multi-region active-active system
questions.prompt: Your service must survive the loss of an entire cloud region and serve users in Europe, the US and India with low latency. Compare active-passive and active-active multi-region designs, and explain data replication across regions, write conflicts, traffic routing, failover and the cost of strong consistency over long distances.

expectedConcepts.label: Requirements and scale estimates
Active-passive vs active-active
Geo routing via DNS/anycast with health checks
Async cross-region replication; RPO > 0
Write conflicts: home region per user, CRDTs, LWW
Strong consistency needs consensus across regions: latency cost
Failover drills, capacity headroom, avoid split brain
Data residency and per-region capacity
Trade-offs: cost and complexity vs availability and latency

questions.modelAnswer: Start with targets: RTO (how fast you recover) and RPO (how much data you may lose), plus latency goals per geography. Active-passive runs everything in one primary region and replicates data to a standby region that takes over on failure; it is simpler, but failover is slow and risky if rarely exercised, and remote users get higher latency. Active-active serves traffic from every region simultaneously: users are routed to the nearest healthy region via geo-DNS or anycast with health checks. The hard part is data. Cross-region replication is usually asynchronous (a write in Mumbai reaches Virginia 100-200 ms later), so a region loss can drop recent writes (RPO > 0), and concurrent writes to the same record in two regions conflict. Avoid conflicts by giving each user or tenant a home region that owns their writes, use CRDTs or last-write-wins only where acceptable, and keep truly global invariants (unique usernames, balances) in a strongly consistent store using consensus across regions such as Spanner or CockroachDB - accepting cross-region round trips on those writes. Each region needs headroom to absorb a failed region's traffic; rehearse failovers regularly and guard against split brain with fencing. Data residency laws may pin data to regions. Trade-off: roughly double cost and much more complexity for higher availability and lower latency.

questions.title: Design an online code judge like LeetCode
questions.prompt: Design a system where users submit code in many languages and get results against hidden test cases within seconds. Focus on secure sandboxing of untrusted code, resource limits, the submission queue and worker fleet, handling contest traffic spikes, and returning results to the user.

expectedConcepts.label: Requirements and scale estimates
Submissions queued; workers pull jobs
Sandbox: containers with seccomp/gVisor/Firecracker, no network
CPU time, memory, process and output limits
Results via polling or WebSocket; store verdicts
Autoscale workers on queue depth; prewarmed sandboxes
Deterministic, fair timing; retries for infra failures
Trade-offs: isolation strength vs startup latency
