Walk through how you would improve retrieval: chunking strategy, embedding model choice, hybrid search with BM25, metadata filtering, query rewriting, re-ranking with a cross-encoder, and how you measure each change.

expectedConcepts.label: Chunk size and overlap; structure-aware chunking
Hybrid dense + BM25 keyword search
Cross-encoder re-ranking of top candidates
Query rewriting, expansion, metadata filters
Measure recall@k on labelled queries; inspect failures

questions.modelAnswer: First measure: label a set of real questions with the passages that answer them and compute recall@k and MRR, so every change is judged by numbers and failures can be inspected. Chunking: chunks that are too large dilute the embedding with unrelated content; too small loses context. Split along document structure (headings, sections, code blocks), use moderate sizes with some overlap, and prepend context such as the document title and section path to each chunk. Embeddings: choose a model that performs well on your domain and language - benchmark a few on your labelled set - and embed queries and documents with the right instructions or prefixes. Dense embeddings miss exact identifiers, error codes, product names and rare terms, so add BM25 keyword search and merge the two result lists with reciprocal rank fusion (hybrid search). Use metadata filters for product, version, language and access permissions. Query processing: rewrite conversational follow-ups into standalone questions using chat history, expand or split complex queries into sub-queries, or generate a hypothetical answer and embed it (HyDE). Re-ranking: retrieve generously (say the top 50) and re-score candidates with a cross-encoder that reads the query and passage together - far more accurate than bi-encoder similarity - then pass only the best few to the model. Each stage adds latency and cost, so keep only what the metrics justify.

questions.title: LLM agents and tool use
questions.prompt: Explain how LLM agents work. Describe tool or function calling, the reason-act loop, planning, memory, and multi-step tasks such as researching a question or fixing a bug in a codebase. Why are agents unreliable, and what design practices make them safer and more effective?

expectedConcepts.label: Tool calling: model emits structured calls, app executes, result fed back
Agent loop: think, act, observe until done
Context management and memory; planning and sub-agents
Errors compound over steps; loops; prompt injection
Practices: good tool design, limits, checkpoints, human approval, evals

questions.modelAnswer: An agent is an LLM placed in a loop with tools. The application describes available tools - search, read file, run tests, query a database, send a message - with names, descriptions and JSON schemas. Given a task, the model either answers or emits a structured tool call; the application executes it and appends the result to the conversation; the model observes it, reasons about the next step and continues until it decides the task is done. This reason-act-observe loop lets the model gather information it lacks and take actions: to fix a bug it might search the codebase, read relevant files, edit one, run the tests, read the failure and iterate. Longer tasks need context management - summarising old steps, storing notes or using sub-agents with fresh contexts - and sometimes an explicit plan. Agents are unreliable because errors compound: a 95%-reliable step repeated 20 times succeeds only about a third of the time; models can loop, give up early, hallucinate tool arguments, or be hijacked by injected instructions in tool results. Practices that help: few, well-designed tools with clear descriptions and helpful error messages; step and cost limits; sandboxed execution; verification steps such as running tests; checkpoints and human approval for irreversible actions; least-privilege credentials; and an evaluation suite of realistic tasks to measure success rates before and after changes.

questions.title: Structured outputs and function calling
questions.prompt: Your application needs an LLM to return data that code can parse reliably, such as extracted invoice fields. Compare asking for JSON in the prompt, JSON mode, schema-constrained decoding and function calling. How does constrained decoding work, and what validation and error handling do you still need?

expectedConcepts.label: Prompt-only JSON is unreliable: extra text, invalid syntax
Constrained decoding masks tokens to follow a grammar/schema
Function calling returns arguments matching a tool schema
Still validate semantically; retry with error feedback
Valid syntax is not correct content; schema design; refusals

questions.modelAnswer: Asking for JSON in the prompt works most of the time, but models sometimes add explanations, wrap output in markdown fences, truncate, or produce invalid syntax, which breaks parsers at scale. JSON mode guarantees syntactically valid JSON but not your schema. Schema-constrained decoding (structured outputs) guarantees that output matches a JSON schema or grammar: at each step, the decoder computes which tokens could continue a valid document from the current state and masks out all others before sampling, so the model physically cannot emit a missing bracket or a wrong field name. Function or tool calling is the same idea framed as invoking a function: the model returns a function name and arguments matching the declared parameter schema. Even with guaranteed structure, the content can be wrong: the model can hallucinate an invoice number, put a date in the wrong field or invent a value instead of admitting it is absent. So design schemas that allow null or "not found" for missing data, include enums and descriptions, and keep schemas reasonably flat. Validate semantically with a library like Zod or Pydantic - types, ranges, cross-field rules, values present in the source text - and on failure retry with the validation error included, or route to human review. Also handle refusals and truncation explicitly, and evaluate extraction accuracy on a labelled set.

questions.title: Quantising large language models
questions.prompt: Explain model quantisation for LLMs. Why does reducing weights from 16-bit to 8 or 4 bits speed up inference and cut memory, what is the difference between weight-only and weight-and-activation quantisation, how do methods like GPTQ and AWQ preserve accuracy, and what are the quality trade-offs?

expectedConcepts.label: Represent weights with fewer bits using scales/zero points
Less memory and bandwidth; decode is memory-bound
Weight-only vs weights+activations; PTQ vs QAT; group-wise scales
GPTQ, AWQ handle outliers and salient weights; FP8
Quality loss grows below 4 bits; evaluate on your tasks

questions.modelAnswer: Model weights are normally stored in 16-bit floating point (FP16 or BF16). Quantisation stores them with fewer bits - 8-bit or 4-bit integers, or FP8 - by mapping ranges of values onto a small set of levels with a scale (and sometimes a zero point) per tensor, per channel or per small group of weights. A 70-billion-parameter model needs about 140 GB in 16-bit but roughly 35-40 GB in 4-bit, so it fits on far fewer GPUs or even a laptop. Speed improves too because token-by-token decoding is memory-bandwidth bound: reading half or a quarter of the bytes per weight makes each step faster, even though values are dequantised for computation. Weight-only quantisation (common for 4-bit) keeps activations in 16-bit; weight-and-activation quantisation (W8A8, FP8) also speeds up the matrix multiplications on hardware that supports low-precision math, which helps the compute-bound prefill phase. Post-training quantisation needs no retraining, but naive rounding hurts accuracy because LLMs have outlier features and some weights matter much more than others. GPTQ quantises layer by layer while compensating for rounding error using second-order information; AWQ protects salient weight channels identified from activation magnitudes; SmoothQuant shifts activation outliers into weights. Quantisation-aware training gives the best low-bit quality. 8-bit is usually near-lossless, 4-bit costs a little, and below 4 bits quality drops noticeably, so evaluate on your own tasks.

questions.title: Serving LLMs efficiently: batching and throughput
questions.prompt: You must serve an open-weights LLM to thousands of users. Explain the latency metrics that matter (time to first token, inter-token latency), why static batching wastes GPU capacity, how continuous batching and paged attention in servers like vLLM work, chunked prefill, speculative decoding, and how you trade throughput against latency.

expectedConcepts.label: TTFT, inter-token latency/TPOT, throughput tokens/s
Batching amortises weight reads; static batching waits for longest
Continuous batching adds/removes requests every step
Paged attention, chunked prefill, prefix caching
Throughput vs latency, tensor parallelism, autoscaling, speculative decoding

questions.modelAnswer: Users feel two latencies: time to first token (dominated by queueing and the prefill of their prompt) and inter-token latency or time per output token (the decode speed, which determines whether text streams smoothly). Operators care about throughput - total tokens per second per GPU - and therefore cost. A decode step for one sequence reads all the model weights to produce a single token, so the GPU is mostly waiting on memory; batching many sequences together reuses each weight read for many tokens, raising throughput dramatically. Static batching groups requests and waits until the longest one finishes, leaving slots idle and forcing new requests to wait. Continuous (iteration-level) batching, introduced by Orca and used in vLLM, TGI and TensorRT-LLM, inserts new requests and removes finished ones at every decode step. The KV cache limits how many sequences fit, so paged attention allocates it in blocks to avoid fragmentation and enable sharing, and prefix caching reuses common prompts. Chunked prefill splits long prompts so they do not stall everyone's decoding. Speculative decoding uses a small draft model to propose several tokens that the large model verifies in one pass, cutting latency without changing outputs. Larger batches raise throughput but slow each user's tokens, so set limits per SLO, use tensor parallelism across GPUs for big models, and autoscale on queue depth.

questions.title: Mixture-of-experts models
questions.prompt: Explain mixture-of-experts transformer architectures. How does a router send each token to a few expert feed-forward networks, why does this give a model many parameters but low compute per token, what are the challenges of load balancing and training stability, and what does MoE mean for memory and serving?

expectedConcepts.label: Many expert FFNs per layer; router picks top-k per token
Sparse activation: total vs active parameters
Load balancing losses, capacity factor, token dropping
All experts must be in memory; expert parallelism; communication
Better quality per FLOP vs memory, routing instability, batching complexity

questions.modelAnswer: In a standard dense transformer every token passes through every parameter. A mixture-of-experts layer replaces the single feed-forward block in some or all layers with many expert feed-forward networks - say 8 to over 100 - plus a small router network. For each token, the router scores the experts and sends the token to the top one or two (or a few of many fine-grained experts), combining their outputs weighted by the router probabilities; attention layers usually stay dense. The model therefore has a huge total parameter count, giving more capacity to store knowledge, while each token uses only a small fraction - its active parameters - so training and inference compute per token resemble a much smaller dense model. Mixtral, for example, has about 47 billion total parameters but roughly 13 billion active per token. Challenges: routers tend to collapse onto a few favourite experts, so training adds auxiliary load-balancing losses or bias adjustments, and experts have capacity limits beyond which tokens may be dropped or rerouted; routing can make training unstable and fine-tuning trickier. For serving, all experts must be held in memory even though few are used per token, so memory needs match the total size; large deployments shard experts across GPUs (expert parallelism), which requires all-to-all communication, and efficiency depends on batching enough tokens to keep every expert busy.

questions.title: Multimodal models: vision-language
questions.prompt: Explain how multimodal models that understand images and text work. Describe how images are turned into tokens with a vision encoder, how those are connected to a language model, contrastive pretraining like CLIP, typical capabilities and failure modes such as counting, fine text and spatial reasoning, and practical uses.

expectedConcepts.label: Vision encoder (ViT) turns image patches into embeddings
Projection/adapter maps image features into the LLM token space
CLIP: contrastive image-text pretraining aligns embeddings
Failures: counting, small text, spatial relations, hallucinated details
Uses: document understanding, charts, UI agents, accessibility

questions.modelAnswer: A typical vision-language model has three parts. A vision encoder, usually a vision transformer, splits an image into patches (for example 14x14 pixels) and turns each into an embedding, producing a sequence of image features. A connector - a linear projection, small MLP or cross-attention module - maps those features into the language model's embedding space so they can be treated like tokens and interleaved with text. The language model then reads the combined sequence and generates text. Vision encoders are often initialised from contrastive pretraining such as CLIP, which trains an image encoder and a text encoder on hundreds of millions of image-caption pairs so matching pairs have similar embeddings and mismatched pairs do not; this alone enables zero-shot classification and image search. The combined model is then trained on captioning, visual question answering and instruction data, and some models are trained natively multimodal from the start. High-resolution images are tiled into crops, which costs many tokens. Capabilities: describing images, reading documents and charts, answering questions about screenshots, and operating user interfaces. Failure modes: counting many objects, reading tiny or dense text, precise spatial relationships and measurements, and confidently describing details that are not there. Uses include document processing, accessibility descriptions, visual QA in support, and computer-use agents.

questions.title: How diffusion models generate images
questions.prompt: Explain how diffusion models such as Stable Diffusion generate images. Describe the forward noising process, training a network to predict noise, the reverse denoising process, latent diffusion with an autoencoder, how text conditioning and classifier-free guidance work, and how the number of sampling steps affects speed and quality.

expectedConcepts.label: Forward process gradually adds Gaussian noise
Network (U-Net/transformer) learns to predict the noise
Sampling iteratively denoises from random noise
Latent diffusion in a compressed space via a VAE
Text conditioning via cross-attention; classifier-free guidance; fewer steps trade-off

questions.modelAnswer: Diffusion models learn to reverse a gradual corruption process. In the forward process, Gaussian noise is added to a training image over many small steps until it becomes pure noise; this needs no learning, and any intermediate noise level can be sampled directly. A neural network - historically a U-Net, increasingly a transformer - is trained to take a noisy image and the noise level and predict the noise that was added (or equivalently the clean image), using a simple mean squared error loss. Generation runs in reverse: start from random noise and repeatedly apply the network to remove a little predicted noise, step by step, until a clean image emerges. Stable Diffusion is a latent diffusion model: an autoencoder first compresses images into a much smaller latent representation, diffusion runs in that latent space, and the decoder turns the final latent into pixels, cutting compute enormously. Text conditioning feeds embeddings from a text encoder (such as CLIP's) into the network through cross-attention. Classifier-free guidance trains the model both with and without the prompt and at sampling time extrapolates from the unconditional prediction toward the conditional one; a higher guidance scale follows the prompt more closely at the cost of diversity and naturalness. Early models needed hundreds of steps; better samplers and distillation (consistency models, few-step variants) now produce good images in a handful of steps, trading some quality for speed.

questions.title: Reducing the cost and latency of LLM applications
questions.prompt: Your LLM-powered feature is too slow and too expensive. Explain the levers you have: choosing smaller models and routing between models, prompt and context trimming, prompt caching, response caching, batching, streaming, parallelising calls, and distillation. How do you make sure quality does not regress?

expectedConcepts.label: Cost and latency scale with input and output tokens
Smaller models and routing/cascades
Prompt (prefix) caching and response caching
Streaming, parallel calls, batch APIs for offline work
Guard quality with evals; distillation/fine-tuning a small model

questions.modelAnswer: Cost and latency are roughly proportional to tokens processed and generated, and to model size; output tokens are slower and usually pricier than input tokens. Levers: use the smallest model that meets the quality bar for each step - many classification, extraction or routing steps do not need a frontier model - and build a cascade where a cheap model handles easy requests and escalates hard or low-confidence ones. Trim the context: shorter system prompts, fewer and better-chosen retrieved chunks, summarising long histories. Ask for concise outputs and set sensible max tokens. Prompt caching (offered by major APIs and serving engines) reuses the processed prefix of long, repeated prompts such as system instructions or documents, cutting both cost and time to first token - so put stable content first. Cache full responses for repeated questions, and consider semantic caching carefully because near-duplicate questions may need different answers. Improve perceived latency by streaming tokens and running independent calls in parallel rather than sequentially; move non-interactive work to discounted batch APIs. For high volume, distil or fine-tune a small model on outputs from a large one. Every change needs an evaluation suite run before shipping, plus monitoring of quality, cost per request and p95 latency in production, because savings that silently reduce answer quality are false economies.

questions.title: Guardrails and safety for LLM applications
questions.prompt: Explain how you would add guardrails to a customer-facing LLM chatbot. Cover input filtering, output moderation, keeping the bot on topic, protecting personal data, preventing harmful or legally risky answers, handling uncertainty honestly, and the trade-off between safety and helpfulness.

expectedConcepts.label: Input checks: abuse, injection attempts, PII, off-topic
Output moderation and policy checks before showing users
Grounding and honest uncertainty; escalation to humans
Scope limits, tool permissions, rate limits, logging
Over-blocking vs harm; measure both; red teaming

questions.modelAnswer: Guardrails are layered checks around the model, not a single prompt. On input: detect abusive content, obvious jailbreak or prompt-injection attempts, and personal data that should be masked before it is sent to a third-party model or logged; classify intent so off-topic requests (a banking bot asked for medical advice) get a polite redirect. In the system prompt and tool design: narrow the bot's scope, give it only the tools and data it needs, and define what it must never do, such as promising refunds or giving legal advice. Ground answers in retrieved, approved content and instruct the model to say it does not know and offer escalation to a human when information is missing, rather than guessing. On output: run moderation for harmful content, check policy rules (no account numbers, no competitor pricing, required disclaimers), verify that cited sources exist, and block or rewrite violations before the user sees them. Operationally: rate limits against abuse, audit logs with privacy controls, monitoring of flagged conversations, and regular red-teaming. Guardrails have their own false positives: over-blocking frustrates users and makes the product useless, so evaluate both harmful-content leakage and wrongful refusals on test sets and tune thresholds deliberately.

questions.title: Chain-of-thought and reasoning models
questions.prompt: Explain chain-of-thought prompting and why asking a model to reason step by step improves performance on maths and logic problems. How do modern reasoning models trained with reinforcement learning extend this with longer thinking, what are test-time compute trade-offs, and what are the limitations of visible reasoning?

expectedConcepts.label: Chain-of-thought: intermediate steps before the answer
More tokens = more computation; decomposes problems
Reasoning models trained with RL on verifiable rewards
Test-time compute: longer thinking, self-consistency, more cost/latency
Limits: unfaithful reasoning, overthinking, cost; not needed for simple tasks

questions.modelAnswer: A transformer does a fixed amount of computation per generated token, so a model answering a multi-step problem in one token has little room to work it out. Chain-of-thought prompting asks the model to write intermediate steps first; each written step becomes context for the next, effectively giving the model more serial computation and a scratchpad, and decomposing the problem into easier pieces. This substantially improves maths, logic and multi-step planning. Self-consistency samples several reasoning paths and takes the majority answer, trading more compute for accuracy. Reasoning models take this further: they are trained with reinforcement learning on problems with verifiable answers (maths, code with tests) to generate long internal reasoning before answering - exploring approaches, checking work, backtracking. Performance then scales with test-time compute: allowing more thinking tokens improves results on hard problems, at the cost of latency and token spend, and many APIs expose a reasoning-effort or budget setting. Limitations: the visible reasoning is not guaranteed to be a faithful account of how the model reached its answer; models can overthink simple questions, wasting time and sometimes talking themselves into errors; and for simple lookups, extraction or classification, a non-reasoning model is faster and cheaper. Use reasoning where problems genuinely require multi-step work.

questions.title: Knowledge distillation for language models
questions.prompt: Explain knowledge distillation: training a small student model to imitate a large teacher. Compare matching soft probability distributions with training on teacher-generated outputs, why soft targets carry more information than labels, how distillation is used to create small capable LLMs, and its limits and legal considerations.

expectedConcepts.label: Student learns to mimic teacher outputs
Soft targets with temperature carry dark knowledge
Sequence-level distillation via synthetic data from the teacher
Uses: small fast models, task-specific students, reasoning traces
Limits: student capacity, inherits teacher errors, terms of service

questions.modelAnswer: Distillation trains a small student model to reproduce the behaviour of a larger, more capable teacher, so you get much of the teacher's quality at a fraction of the inference cost. In classic distillation (Hinton et al.), the student is trained to match the teacher's full output probability distribution, softened with a temperature, usually alongside the true labels. These soft targets contain "dark knowledge": a teacher that says an image is 80% dog, 15% wolf and 0.01% car teaches similarity structure that a one-hot label cannot, giving the student a richer signal per example. For LLMs, logit-level distillation minimises the KL divergence between teacher and student next-token distributions, which requires access to the teacher's logits and compatible tokenizers. The more common approach is sequence-level distillation: use the teacher to generate large amounts of high-quality responses, explanations or reasoning traces for many prompts, and fine-tune the student on that synthetic data. Many small open models and task-specific production models are built this way, and reasoning abilities can be partly transferred by training on teacher reasoning traces. Limits: a student with far fewer parameters cannot absorb everything, especially broad factual knowledge; it inherits the teacher's biases and mistakes; and generating training data from a proprietary model may violate its terms of service, so check licences.

questions.title: Speculative decoding
questions.prompt: Explain speculative decoding for faster LLM inference. How does a small draft model propose several tokens that the large target model verifies in a single forward pass, why the output distribution stays exactly the same as the target model's, what determines the speed-up, and variants such as Medusa heads and n-gram or prompt-lookup drafting.

expectedConcepts.label: Draft model proposes k tokens cheaply
Target verifies all k in one parallel pass
Rejection sampling keeps output distribution identical
Speed-up depends on acceptance rate and draft cost; decode is memory-bound
Medusa heads, EAGLE, prompt lookup / n-gram drafting

questions.modelAnswer: Decoding is slow because each token requires a full forward pass of the large model, and that pass is memory-bandwidth bound - the GPU spends most of its time reading weights, with spare compute. Verifying several tokens costs about the same as generating one, because a forward pass over k positions processes them in parallel. Speculative decoding exploits this: a small, fast draft model proposes the next k tokens (say 4-8); the large target model runs once over the context plus those k tokens, producing its own probability distribution at each position. Draft tokens are accepted left to right using a rejection-sampling rule - accept token t with probability min(1, p_target / p_draft) - and at the first rejection the target samples a replacement from a corrected distribution, so the final output follows exactly the target model's distribution: it is lossless, not an approximation. Each verification pass yields at least one token and up to k + 1. The speed-up depends on how often the target agrees with the draft (high for predictable text like code or boilerplate) and on how cheap the draft is; 2-3x is typical. Variants avoid a separate draft model: Medusa and EAGLE add lightweight extra heads to predict several future tokens, self-speculative methods skip layers, and prompt-lookup or n-gram drafting copies spans from the prompt, which works very well for editing and summarisation where output repeats input.

questions.title: Hypermedia, HATEOAS and the REST maturity model
questions.prompt: Explain the Richardson maturity model for REST APIs and what HATEOAS - hypermedia as the engine of application state - means. Show what links in a response look like, what benefits they promise, and why most real-world APIs stop short of full hypermedia.

expectedConcepts.label: Richardson levels 0-3: RPC, resources, HTTP verbs, hypermedia
Responses include links to available actions
Benefits: discoverability, server-controlled workflows, evolvable URLs
Formats: HAL, JSON:API, Siren; pagination links
Why rare: clients hard-code anyway, verbosity, tooling; partial use

questions.modelAnswer: Leonard Richardson described levels of REST adoption. Level 0 tunnels everything through one endpoint, like RPC over HTTP POST. Level 1 introduces resources with their own URLs. Level 2 uses HTTP methods and status codes properly - where most "REST" APIs live. Level 3 adds hypermedia controls: HATEOAS, the idea that responses tell the client what it can do next through links, just as web pages contain links and forms. An order response might include "_links": {"self": {"href": "/orders/42"}, "cancel": {"href": "/orders/42/cancellation", "method": "POST"}, "payment": {"href": "/orders/42/payment"}}, and the cancel link appears only while cancellation is allowed. The promised benefits: clients discover capabilities instead of hard-coding URL patterns and business rules, the server can change URLs and workflows without breaking clients, and the available links describe the resource's state machine. Formats such as HAL, JSON:API and Siren standardise links. In practice most APIs adopt only pieces - self links and next/prev pagination links are common - because client developers still hard-code flows against documentation, generic hypermedia clients never became widespread, responses get more verbose, and OpenAPI-based tooling and code generation assume fixed URL templates.

questions.title: IPv6: why and how
questions.prompt: Explain why IPv6 was created and how it differs from IPv4. Describe the 128-bit address format and notation, how devices get addresses with SLAAC or DHCPv6, why NAT is not needed, how the header and features differ, and why the transition has taken decades, including dual-stack networks.

expectedConcepts.label: IPv4 exhaustion of ~4.3 billion addresses
128-bit addresses in hexadecimal groups; :: shortening
SLAAC and DHCPv6; link-local addresses
End-to-end addressing without NAT; firewalls still needed
Transition: dual stack, tunnels, NAT64; slow adoption; India high adoption

questions.modelAnswer: IPv4 addresses are 32 bits, about 4.3 billion in total - far too few for every phone, laptop and sensor - and the regional registries effectively ran out in the 2010s, kept going only by NAT and address trading. IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses, written as eight groups of four hexadecimal digits separated by colons, with leading zeros dropped and one run of zero groups shortened to "::" - for example 2001:db8::1. The space is so large that every device can have globally unique addresses; a typical home gets a /56 or /64 prefix. Devices can configure themselves using stateless address autoconfiguration (SLAAC) from router advertisements, or use DHCPv6, and every interface also has a link-local address for the local network. Because addresses are plentiful, NAT is unnecessary and end-to-end connectivity returns, which simplifies peer-to-peer and VoIP - but a stateful firewall is still needed for security. The header is simpler and fixed-size, routers no longer fragment packets, ARP is replaced by neighbour discovery, and broadcast is replaced by multicast. Adoption took decades because IPv4 and IPv6 are not directly compatible: networks run dual stack, translation such as NAT64 bridges them, and every device, application and ISP must support it. Mobile networks drove adoption; India is among the countries with the highest IPv6 usage.

questions.title: Partial failures, gray failures and network partitions in practice
questions.prompt: Real distributed systems rarely fail cleanly. Explain partial and gray failures - a node that answers health checks but serves requests slowly, an asymmetric network partition, or a disk that is slowly failing. Why do these defeat simple failure detection, how do they cause cascading outages, and what designs and observability help?

expectedConcepts.label: Gray failure: component appears healthy to some observers but not others
Examples: slow disk, packet loss, asymmetric partition, overloaded dependency
Simple heartbeats miss them; use request-level signals and outlier detection
Cascades via retries, timeouts, thread pool exhaustion
Designs: deep health checks, timeouts, circuit breakers, bulkheads, fail fast

questions.modelAnswer: Textbook failures are clean: a node crashes and stops responding. Production failures are often partial. In a gray failure a component looks healthy to one observer and broken to another: a server answers the load balancer's lightweight health check but times out on real requests because its disk is degrading, a dependency is overloaded, or one network link drops 5% of packets. Partitions can be asymmetric - A can reach B but not the reverse - or partial, where some nodes see each other and others do not. These defeat simple heartbeat-based detection because the heartbeat path is fine; the cluster keeps routing traffic to the sick node, and consensus or leader election may behave strangely when nodes disagree about who is alive. Gray failures often trigger cascades: callers block on slow responses, thread or connection pools fill up, retries multiply load, and the slowness spreads upstream until a whole service is down. Defences: health checks that exercise real dependencies (carefully, so one bad dependency does not mark everything unhealthy), outlier detection that ejects instances with elevated error rates or latency as measured by their callers, strict timeouts and deadlines, circuit breakers and bulkheads that isolate pools per dependency, failing fast instead of queueing, and observability from the client's perspective - per-instance latency percentiles and error rates - because the system's own view of itself is exactly what gray failures fool.
